chunks: From him, from Al-Jamourani, from Ibn Abi Hamza, from Sayf ibn Amira, from Is'haq ibn Ammar, from Abu Baseer, who said:

I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and he said to me: 'O Abu Muhammad, go with us to visit Ismail, for he has been complaining.' So we arose and entered upon Ismail, and there was a Fakhta (ring-dove) in a cage in his house, shrieking. So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'O my son, what calls you to keep this Fakhta? Do you not know that it is inauspicious? Do you not know what it is saying?' Ismail said, 'No.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is supplicating against its owners, saying: We are lost, we are lost! Therefore exit it.'

key_terms.تَدْعُو: Supplicating or calling out (in a spiritual sense)
key_terms.فَاخِتَة: A type of ring-dove, specifically noted in this context for its call

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the Fakhta bird's call in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam Ali ibn Abi al-Hadi (peace be upon him) visits the sick Ismail ibn Jushan and observes a caged ring-dove (*Fakhta*), explaining that its chirping is a supplication against its owners, rendering the bird inauspicious (*mashumah*). This narration highlights the Shia belief in the spiritual awareness of animals and the concept of *du'a* (supplication) even from non-human creatures, linking physical possession to spiritual consequence. It serves as a practical example of how everyday observations in the domestic sphere reflect deeper metaphysical realities in Shia tradition.
